Windswept describes something that has been exposed to strong, persistent wind — and shows it. The word is built from two ideas: wind (moving air) and swept (the past tense of "sweep," meaning to pass over a surface forcefully and continuously). So when you call something windswept, you are saying that the wind has swept over it — powerfully, repeatedly, and noticeably.
The two main ways it is used

1. Describing places and landscapes

This is the most common and most powerful use. A windswept place is one that is open, exposed, and battered by the wind. There are no natural shelters — no tall buildings, dense forests, or mountains to block the wind. The wind arrives freely and with full force.

Think of:

  • A bare clifftop above the sea
  • A treeless highland moor
  • An open beach in winter
  • A mountain summit
  • A remote prairie

These places feel raw and wild. When you stand in a windswept location, you feel the wind as a constant presence — it pushes against you, rushes past your ears, and dominates the environment. The word often implies a kind of dramatic, elemental power. Nature is in charge there.

"She stood on the windswept hillside, looking out over the grey sea."

"The windswept coastline was beautiful but brutal in winter."

2. Describing the appearance of things shaped or tossed by wind

Here, windswept describes how something looks after the wind has acted on it — either over a long time (permanently shaping it) or in the recent moment (temporarily messing it up).

Trees and vegetation: A windswept tree is one that the wind has permanently bent and shaped. If strong winds blow from one direction year after year, a tree's trunk leans away from the wind, and its branches all grow to one side, as if being blown even when the air is still. The tree has been sculpted by the wind. This is one of the most vivid and classic uses of the word.

"A lone windswept pine clung to the edge of the cliff."

Hair: Windswept hair is hair that the wind has blown around — tousled, disheveled, out of place. It looks the way hair looks when you have been out in strong wind: loosened from its style, slightly wild, blown across the face.

"He arrived at the door with a red nose and windswept hair."

This use can sometimes carry a slightly attractive, fresh, or adventurous quality — the look of someone who has just come in from the outdoors. But it can also simply mean messy and untidy, depending on context.

Clothing and objects: Less commonly, things like coats, flags, or sand dunes can be called windswept when they have been visibly pushed, shaped, or scattered by wind.
The feeling and atmosphere the word carries

Words carry not just meaning but also a mood — and windswept is a particularly atmospheric word. It almost always brings a sense of:

  • Wildness and rawness: There is something untamed about a windswept place. It has not been softened or controlled. Nature is present and strong.
  • Openness and exposure: A windswept place is never enclosed or sheltered. Everything is out in the open, under the sky.
  • Remoteness or solitude: Windswept places tend to be far from cities and crowds. They feel lonely, sometimes desolate, but often in a way that is more grand than sad.
  • Drama and beauty: Writers and poets use windswept to evoke romantic, dramatic landscapes — the Scottish Highlands, the Irish coast, the American Great Plains, the Patagonian steppe. The word has a literary, almost cinematic quality.

Because of this, windswept is not a neutral word. It does not merely state a fact about wind; it paints a picture and sets a mood.
When the word has a slightly negative tone

While windswept is often used admiringly, it can sometimes carry a note of bleakness or discomfort. A windswept wasteland, a windswept winter street, or a windswept industrial estate does not sound appealing — it sounds cold, bare, and harsh. The word then suggests a place that is unpleasantly exposed and lacking any warmth or protection.

So the emotional tone of windswept depends on what it is describing. Applied to a dramatic coastline or rugged highland, it feels magnificent. Applied to a flat car park or a bleak town square, it can sound dreary.

To use the word confidently, remember this: windswept means visibly shaped by, exposed to, or tossed by strong wind. It describes a place that the wind rules over, a tree or landscape permanently marked by the wind's force, or hair and appearance made messy or wild by the wind. It almost always carries a feeling of wildness, openness, and natural power — and whether that feels beautiful or bleak depends on what is being described.

If you picture someone standing on a rugged sea cliff, hair blowing back, the cold wind roaring in off the ocean, the grass flattening around them, and one lone tree nearby bent permanently sideways — that entire scene, every part of it, could be called windswept.
